items.stem: Which of the following best describes "market demand"?
options: An equation of the form Qd = a − bP showing quantity demanded as a function of price, where a is the quantity-axis intercept and b gives the change in Qd per $1 change in price
As a consumer consumes more units of a good, the extra satisfaction from each additional unit eventually falls
The inverse relationship between the price of a good and the quantity demanded, ceteris paribus
The sum of all individual consumers' demands for a good at each price
items.answer: The sum of all individual consumers' demands for a good at each price
items.markingKey: D. "market demand" is the sum of all individual consumers' demands for a good at each price.

items.stem: Mateo writes: "When the price of a good falls, demand increases." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A fall in the good's own price increases the quantity demanded (a movement along the curve), not demand; demand only increases when a non-price determinant shifts the curve right.
items.markingKey: A fall in the good's own price increases the quantity demanded (a movement along the curve), not demand; demand only increases when a non-price determinant shifts the curve right. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why demand must be 'effective' to be shown on a demand curve.
items.answer: A demand curve shows quantities consumers are willing and able to buy; wanting a good without the purchasing power to buy it does not affect the market. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A demand curve shows quantities consumers are willing and able to buy; wanting a good without the purchasing power to buy it does not affect the market. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using the law of demand, explain what would happen to the number of rides taken on the Singapore MRT if fares rose by 10%, ceteris paribus.
items.answer: The quantity demanded of MRT rides would fall (movement up along the demand curve) as rides become more expensive relative to buses or taxis and real incomes fall.
items.markingKey: The quantity demanded of MRT rides would fall (movement up along the demand curve) as rides become more expensive relative to buses or taxis and real incomes fall.

items.stem: The weekly demand schedules of the three buyers of electric scooters in a village market are – Ana: $2 → 7, $4 → 5, $6 → 3, $8 → 1; Omar: $2 → 9, $4 → 5, $6 → 1, $8 → 0; Diego: $2 → 12, $4 → 8, $6 → 4, $8 → 0. Calculate market quantity demanded at $6 and at $2, and explain how your answers illustrate the law of demand.
items.markingKey: Sum each column: 8 and 28 [2]; quantity demanded is higher at the lower price, an inverse relationship ceteris paribus [2].

items.stem: Using Netflix's price increases and password-sharing crackdown in 2023 as an example, explain the law of demand.
items.answer: Netflix raised subscription prices in several markets; some users cancelled, though sign-ups rose after password-sharing rules made more people pay for their own accounts. Higher prices reduced the quantity of subscriptions demanded by some consumers, while the rule change (a non-price factor) created new paying demand.
items.markingKey: Context (Netflix raised subscription prices in several markets; some users cancelled, though sign-ups rose after password-sharing rules made more people pay for their own accounts.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Higher prices reduced the quantity of subscriptions demanded by some consumers, while the rule change (a non-price factor) created new paying demand. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the law of demand.

items.stem: Explain why a market demand curve may be flatter than an individual's demand curve for a good such as cinema tickets.
items.answer: Market demand adds quantities across consumers; at lower prices more consumers enter the market (those who would buy none at higher prices), so total quantity responds more to price than one person's demand, making the market curve flatter.
items.markingKey: Market demand adds quantities across consumers; at lower prices more consumers enter the market (those who would buy none at higher prices), so total quantity responds more to price than one person's demand, making the market curve flatter.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, discuss the claim that the law of demand applies to all goods.
items.answer: The law of demand holds for the vast majority of goods; exceptions are rare and usually short-lived.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: substitution and income effects work for nearly all goods; strong empirical support across markets. Arguments against: Veblen (status) goods may be demanded more at higher prices; Giffen goods in extreme poverty (Jensen and Miller's study of rice in China); expectations of further price rises (speculative demand). Judgement: The law of demand holds for the vast majority of goods; exceptions are rare and usually short-lived. Credit relevant diagrams and specific real-world examples. Level 1 (1-3) little understanding.

items.stem: Explain why the demand curve is drawn for a given time period.
items.answer: Quantity demanded is a flow (e.g. per week); without a time period, quantities cannot be compared, and other determinants are more likely to change over longer periods.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Quantity demanded is a flow (e.g. per week); without a time period, quantities cannot be compared, and other determinants are more likely to change over longer periods. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why demand must be 'effective' to be shown on a demand curve.
items.answer: A demand curve shows quantities consumers are willing and able to buy; wanting a good without the purchasing power to buy it does not affect the market.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A demand curve shows quantities consumers are willing and able to buy; wanting a good without the purchasing power to buy it does not affect the market. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the source below.

A survey of 400 students in Vienna found that at a price of €3 per coffee they would buy 2,600 coffees a week from the campus café. When the price fell to €2.50 in a promotion, purchases rose to 3,100 coffees a week.
— Hypothetical student survey

Using the data, explain how it illustrates the law of demand.
items.answer: As the price fell from €3 to €2.50, quantity demanded rose from 2,600 to 3,100 a week, ceteris paribus – an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded (a movement down along the demand curve).
items.markingKey: As the price fell from €3 to €2.50, quantity demanded rose from 2,600 to 3,100 a week, ceteris paribus – an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded (a movement down along the demand curve). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.markingKey: A fall in the good's own price increases the quantity demanded (a movement along the curve), not demand; demand only increases when a non-price determinant shifts the curve right. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "substitutes".
items.answer: Goods that can be used in place of each other, so a rise in the price of one increases demand for the other
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: goods that can be used in place of each other, so a rise in the price of one increases demand for the other. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why an expected future price rise can increase demand today.
items.answer: If consumers expect prices to rise (e.g. before a tax increase), they bring forward purchases to avoid paying more later, so demand at every current price rises and the curve shifts right.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If consumers expect prices to rise (e.g. before a tax increase), they bring forward purchases to avoid paying more later, so demand at every current price rises and the curve shifts right. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Zara writes: "Inferior goods are goods of poor quality." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: 'Inferior' refers only to how demand responds to income: demand falls as income rises. Many inferior goods (e.g. bus travel in some cities) are perfectly good quality.
items.markingKey: 'Inferior' refers only to how demand responds to income: demand falls as income rises. Many inferior goods (e.g. bus travel in some cities) are perfectly good quality. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

Sales of electric vehicles in Norway reached about 80% of new car sales in 2022. The government exempted EVs from VAT and purchase taxes, allowed them to use bus lanes and cut toll charges, while petrol prices rose sharply.
— Extract based on reporting of Norway's EV policies

Using the extract, identify two non-price determinants that increased demand for electric vehicles and explain their effect.
items.answer: Higher petrol prices (substitute became dearer) and non-price benefits such as bus-lane access (tastes/preferences) shifted EV demand right; tax exemptions lowered the price, a movement along the demand curve.
items.markingKey: Higher petrol prices (substitute became dearer) and non-price benefits such as bus-lane access (tastes/preferences) shifted EV demand right; tax exemptions lowered the price, a movement along the demand curve. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Briefly describe the rapid growth of oat milk sales in Europe and the US and explain what it reveals about a change in tastes and preferences as a non-price determinant of demand.
items.answer: Sales of plant-based milks rose strongly in the late 2010s as consumers became more concerned about health, animal welfare and climate change. Changing preferences increased demand for oat milk at every price (rightward shift), while demand for dairy milk fell.
items.markingKey: Context (Sales of plant-based milks rose strongly in the late 2010s as consumers became more concerned about health, animal welfare and climate change.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Changing preferences increased demand for oat milk at every price (rightward shift), while demand for dairy milk fell. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a change in tastes and preferences as a non-price determinant of demand.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Advertising is the most effective way for firms to increase the demand for their products.
items.answer: Advertising can shift demand, especially for differentiated consumer goods, but its effectiveness is limited compared with income and quality changes.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shifts demand right by changing tastes and awareness; builds brand loyalty, making demand less price elastic. Arguments against: income and the prices of substitutes have larger effects; advertising is costly and its effects can be short-lived; product quality, innovation and word of mouth matter more for many goods. Supported judgement: Advertising can shift demand, especially for differentiated consumer goods, but its effectiveness is limited compared with income and quality changes.

items.stem: Define the term "inferior good".
items.answer: A good for which demand falls when consumers' income increases, because consumers switch to better alternatives
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a good for which demand falls when consumers' income increases, because consumers switch to better alternatives. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between complements and substitutes.
items.answer: Substitutes are used instead of each other, so a rise in one's price raises demand for the other; complements are used together, so a rise in one's price lowers demand for the other.
items.markingKey: Substitutes are used instead of each other, so a rise in one's price raises demand for the other; complements are used together, so a rise in one's price lowers demand for the other. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In 2020 demand for home-workout equipment rose sharply. Identify the non-price determinant that changed and state the effect on the demand curve.
items.answer: Tastes and preferences (and the closure of gyms, which are substitutes) changed in favour of home exercise; demand shifted to the right.
items.markingKey: Tastes and preferences (and the closure of gyms, which are substitutes) changed in favour of home exercise; demand shifted to the right.

items.stem: A student claims that a fall in the price of a good shifts its demand curve to the right. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the demand curve; only non-price determinants shift it.
items.markingKey: A change in the good's own price causes a movement along the demand curve; only non-price determinants shift it. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Define the term "substitution effect".
items.answer: The change in quantity demanded resulting from the good becoming relatively cheaper or dearer compared with substitutes
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the change in quantity demanded resulting from the good becoming relatively cheaper or dearer compared with substitutes. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between marginal utility and total utility.
items.answer: Total utility is the overall satisfaction from all units consumed; marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from the last unit.
items.markingKey: Total utility is the overall satisfaction from all units consumed; marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from the last unit. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between total utility and marginal utility.
items.answer: Total utility is the overall satisfaction from all units consumed; marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from the last unit.
items.markingKey: Total utility is the overall satisfaction from all units consumed; marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from the last unit. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mohammed's total utility (in utils) from mangoes per day is: 1 unit: 23, 2 units: 44, 3 units: 63, 4 units: 66. Calculate the marginal utility of unit 4.
items.answer: 3 utils

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how the law of diminishing marginal utility leads to a downward-sloping demand curve.
items.answer: Diagram 1: marginal utility (vertical) against quantity consumed (horizontal), a downward-sloping MU curve. Diagram 2: price against quantity, downward-sloping demand. Because each unit gives less extra satisfaction, the price consumers are willing to pay for each extra unit falls, so the demand curve slopes down; the consumer buys up to the point where marginal benefit equals price.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram 1: marginal utility (vertical) against quantity consumed (horizontal), a downward-sloping MU curve. Diagram 2: price against quantity, downward-sloping demand. Because each unit gives less extra satisfaction, the price consumers are willing to pay for each extra unit falls, so the demand curve slopes down; the consumer buys up to the point where marginal benefit equals price. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that the income effect is more important than the substitution effect in explaining the law of demand.
items.answer: For most goods the substitution effect dominates; the income effect matters mainly for goods that take a large share of the budget.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: for goods taking a large share of income (housing, rice for the poor) real income changes are large. Arguments against: for most goods the share of income is small, so the income effect is tiny; the substitution effect always works in the direction of the law of demand; for inferior goods the income effect works against the law of demand. Supported judgement: For most goods the substitution effect dominates; the income effect matters mainly for goods that take a large share of the budget.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "total utility"?
options: Factors other than the good's own price that shift the demand curve: income, tastes and preferences, prices of related goods, future price expectations and the number of consumers
A desire to buy a good that is backed by the ability to pay
The total satisfaction a consumer gains from consuming a given quantity of a good
A good for which demand falls when consumers' income increases, because consumers switch to better alternatives
items.answer: The total satisfaction a consumer gains from consuming a given quantity of a good
items.markingKey: C. "total utility" is the total satisfaction a consumer gains from consuming a given quantity of a good.

items.stem: Explain the difference between marginal utility and total utility.
items.answer: Total utility is the overall satisfaction from all units consumed; marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from the last unit.
items.markingKey: Total utility is the overall satisfaction from all units consumed; marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from the last unit. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why a café might offer a second slice of cake at half price, using the concept of diminishing marginal utility.
items.answer: The second slice gives less extra satisfaction than the first, so customers are only willing to pay a lower price for it; the discount persuades them to buy an extra unit.
items.markingKey: The second slice gives less extra satisfaction than the first, so customers are only willing to pay a lower price for it; the discount persuades them to buy an extra unit.

items.stem: With reference to all-you-can-eat buffets, explain how it illustrates diminishing marginal utility.
items.answer: Diners eat until the satisfaction from another plate is very low or zero, because each extra plate has a zero price. Consumers keep eating while marginal utility is positive; because the price of extra food is zero they stop only when MU falls to zero.
items.markingKey: Context (Diners eat until the satisfaction from another plate is very low or zero, because each extra plate has a zero price.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Consumers keep eating while marginal utility is positive; because the price of extra food is zero they stop only when MU falls to zero. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to diminishing marginal utility.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "linear demand function".
items.answer: An equation of the form Qd = a − bP showing quantity demanded as a function of price, where a is the quantity-axis intercept and b gives the change in Qd per $1 change in price
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an equation of the form Qd = a − bP showing quantity demanded as a function of price, where a is the quantity-axis intercept and b gives the change in Qd per $1 change in price. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a change in 'b' changes the steepness of the demand curve.
items.answer: b measures how much quantity demanded responds to a $1 price change; a larger b means a bigger response, so with P on the vertical axis the curve is flatter.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: b measures how much quantity demanded responds to a $1 price change; a larger b means a bigger response, so with P on the vertical axis the curve is flatter. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that if 'b' increases, the demand curve shifts to the right. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A change in b changes the slope (responsiveness), not the position; the curve pivots around the quantity intercept.
items.markingKey: A change in b changes the slope (responsiveness), not the position; the curve pivots around the quantity intercept. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The weekly demand for streaming subscriptions in Oslo is given by Qd = 40 − 2P (P in $, Q in units). Calculate the quantity demanded when the price is $1.
items.markingKey: Qd = 40 − 2 × 1 = 38. [1] substitution [1] answer.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate how a demand function Qd = a − bP is plotted, and how a change in income for a normal good changes the function and the diagram, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram: P on the vertical axis, Q on the horizontal; the curve meets the Q axis at a and the P axis at a/b. A rise in income raises a to a′: the curve shifts right parallel (same slope −1/b), with a higher price intercept a′/b.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: P on the vertical axis, Q on the horizontal; the curve meets the Q axis at a and the P axis at a/b. A rise in income raises a to a′: the curve shifts right parallel (same slope −1/b), with a higher price intercept a′/b. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: A firm estimates demand for its product to be Qd = 900 − 30P. Explain what the values 900 and 30 represent and describe how the demand curve would change if a successful advertising campaign raised quantity demanded by 150 units at every price.
items.answer: 900: quantity demanded when price is zero (non-price determinants); 30: quantity demanded falls by 30 units for each $1 rise in price; new function Qd = 1,050 − 30P: parallel shift to the right, price intercept rises from $30 to $35.
items.markingKey: 900: quantity demanded when price is zero (non-price determinants); 30: quantity demanded falls by 30 units for each $1 rise in price; new function Qd = 1,050 − 30P: parallel shift to the right, price intercept rises from $30 to $35.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An equation of the form Qd = a − bP showing quantity demanded as a function of price, where a is the quantity-axis intercept and b gives the change in Qd per $1 change in price"?
options: non-price determinants of demand
linear demand function
effective demand
price intercept of a linear demand curve
items.answer: linear demand function
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of linear demand function.

items.stem: Priya writes: "In Qd = 100 − 5P, the curve crosses the price axis at P = 100." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Quantity demanded is zero when 5P = 100, so the price intercept is P = 20; 100 is the quantity intercept.
items.markingKey: Quantity demanded is zero when 5P = 100, so the price intercept is P = 20; 100 is the quantity intercept. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe estimating demand functions for public transport and explain what it reveals about the use of linear demand functions.
items.answer: Transport authorities estimate how many journeys are made at different fares, often with linear approximations, to predict the impact of fare changes. A function Qd = a − bP lets planners predict ridership and revenue at different fares; a change in a (e.g. population growth) shifts the function.
items.markingKey: Context (Transport authorities estimate how many journeys are made at different fares, often with linear approximations, to predict the impact of fare changes.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A function Qd = a − bP lets planners predict ridership and revenue at different fares; a change in a (e.g. population growth) shifts the function. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the use of linear demand functions.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that firms should rely on estimated demand functions when setting prices.
items.answer: Demand functions are a useful guide but should be combined with market testing and judgement about rivals and changing conditions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: give clear predictions of sales at different prices; allow calculation of revenue-maximising prices. Arguments against: estimates may be inaccurate or outdated; rivals' reactions are not included; non-price factors change. Judgement: Demand functions are a useful guide but should be combined with market testing and judgement about rivals and changing conditions. options: quantity demanded
marginal utility

law of demand
items.answer: law of demand
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of law of demand.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Goods that are used together, so a rise in the price of one reduces demand for the other"?
options: complements
marginal utility
market demand
price intercept of a linear demand curve
items.answer: complements
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of complements.

items.stem: When the price of a normal good falls, which of the following is true?
options: The income effect reduces quantity demanded
Both effects reduce quantity demanded
Only the substitution effect increases quantity demanded
The income and substitution effects both increase quantity demanded
items.answer: The income and substitution effects both increase quantity demanded
items.markingKey: D. Lower price raises real income and makes the good relatively cheaper; for a normal good both raise quantity demanded.

items.stem: A student claims that in Qd = 100 − 5P, the curve crosses the price axis at P = 100. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Quantity demanded is zero when 5P = 100, so the price intercept is P = 20; 100 is the quantity intercept.
items.markingKey: Quantity demanded is zero when 5P = 100, so the price intercept is P = 20; 100 is the quantity intercept. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between market demand and individual demand.
items.answer: Individual demand is one consumer's willingness and ability to buy at each price; market demand is the sum of all individual quantities demanded at each price.
items.markingKey: Individual demand is one consumer's willingness and ability to buy at each price; market demand is the sum of all individual quantities demanded at each price. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: 'Inferior' refers only to how demand responds to income: demand falls as income rises. Many inferior goods (e.g. bus travel in some cities) are perfectly good quality.
items.markingKey: 'Inferior' refers only to how demand responds to income: demand falls as income rises. Many inferior goods (e.g. bus travel in some cities) are perfectly good quality. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that Diminishing marginal utility means total utility falls as more is consumed. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Diminishing marginal utility means each extra unit adds less satisfaction; total utility still rises as long as marginal utility is positive.
items.markingKey: Diminishing marginal utility means each extra unit adds less satisfaction; total utility still rises as long as marginal utility is positive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the price intercept and the quantity intercept.
items.answer: The quantity intercept (a) is quantity demanded when P = 0; the price intercept (a/b) is the price at which quantity demanded falls to zero.
items.markingKey: The quantity intercept (a) is quantity demanded when P = 0; the price intercept (a/b) is the price at which quantity demanded falls to zero. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between quantity demanded and demand.
items.answer: Demand is the whole relationship between price and quantity (the entire curve); quantity demanded is the amount demanded at one specific price (a point on the curve).
items.markingKey: Demand is the whole relationship between price and quantity (the entire curve); quantity demanded is the amount demanded at one specific price (a point on the curve). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Inferior goods are goods of poor quality." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: 'Inferior' refers only to how demand responds to income: demand falls as income rises. Many inferior goods (e.g. bus travel in some cities) are perfectly good quality.
items.markingKey: 'Inferior' refers only to how demand responds to income: demand falls as income rises. Many inferior goods (e.g. bus travel in some cities) are perfectly good quality. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Diminishing marginal utility means total utility falls as more is consumed." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Diminishing marginal utility means each extra unit adds less satisfaction; total utility still rises as long as marginal utility is positive.
items.markingKey: Diminishing marginal utility means each extra unit adds less satisfaction; total utility still rises as long as marginal utility is positive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how a demand function Qd = a − bP is plotted, and how a change in income for a normal good changes the function and the diagram.
items.answer: Diagram: P on the vertical axis, Q on the horizontal; the curve meets the Q axis at a and the P axis at a/b. A rise in income raises a to a′: the curve shifts right parallel (same slope −1/b), with a higher price intercept a′/b.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram: P on the vertical axis, Q on the horizontal; the curve meets the Q axis at a and the P axis at a/b. A rise in income raises a to a′: the curve shifts right parallel (same slope −1/b), with a higher price intercept a′/b. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: Nia writes: "The market demand curve is found by adding together the prices that each consumer would pay." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Market demand is found by adding the quantities demanded by each consumer at each price – a horizontal summation.
items.markingKey: Market demand is found by adding the quantities demanded by each consumer at each price – a horizontal summation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline the effect of a fall in consumer incomes on the demand for a normal good and an inferior good.
items.answer: Two diagrams: P vs Q. Normal good (e.g. restaurant meals): demand shifts left from D1 to D2, equilibrium price and quantity fall. Inferior good (e.g. bus travel or discount supermarket brands): demand shifts right from D1 to D2, price and quantity rise. Income is a non-price determinant, so the curves shift.

items.stem: Using all-you-can-eat buffets as an example, explain diminishing marginal utility.
items.answer: Diners eat until the satisfaction from another plate is very low or zero, because each extra plate has a zero price. Consumers keep eating while marginal utility is positive; because the price of extra food is zero they stop only when MU falls to zero.
items.markingKey: Context (Diners eat until the satisfaction from another plate is very low or zero, because each extra plate has a zero price.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Consumers keep eating while marginal utility is positive; because the price of extra food is zero they stop only when MU falls to zero. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to diminishing marginal utility.

items.stem: Outline one way in which estimating demand functions for public transport shows the use of linear demand functions.
items.answer: Transport authorities estimate how many journeys are made at different fares, often with linear approximations, to predict the impact of fare changes. A function Qd = a − bP lets planners predict ridership and revenue at different fares; a change in a (e.g. population growth) shifts the function.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that the law of demand applies to all goods.
items.answer: The law of demand holds for the vast majority of goods; exceptions are rare and usually short-lived.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: substitution and income effects work for nearly all goods; strong empirical support across markets. Arguments against: Veblen (status) goods may be demanded more at higher prices; Giffen goods in extreme poverty (Jensen and Miller's study of rice in China); expectations of further price rises (speculative demand). Supported judgement: The law of demand holds for the vast majority of goods; exceptions are rare and usually short-lived.

items.stem: Using demand diagrams, explain the effect of a large rise in the price of air travel on the demand for (i) international hotel rooms and (ii) high-speed rail travel within Europe.
items.answer: (i) hotels are complements to air travel: demand shifts left, lower price and quantity; (ii) rail is a substitute: demand shifts right, higher price and quantity. Each diagram: P/Q axes, original D1 and new D2, new equilibrium.
items.markingKey: (i) hotels are complements to air travel: demand shifts left, lower price and quantity; (ii) rail is a substitute: demand shifts right, higher price and quantity. Each diagram: P/Q axes, original D1 and new D2, new equilibrium.

items.stem: Using the income and substitution effects, explain why a fall in the price of a normal good leads to a larger increase in quantity demanded than a fall in the price of an inferior good.
items.answer: For a normal good both effects increase quantity demanded; for an inferior good the substitution effect raises quantity demanded but the income effect works the other way (higher real income reduces demand), so the net increase is smaller.
items.markingKey: For a normal good both effects increase quantity demanded; for an inferior good the substitution effect raises quantity demanded but the income effect works the other way (higher real income reduces demand), so the net increase is smaller.

items.stem: "Firms should rely on estimated demand functions when setting prices." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Demand functions are a useful guide but should be combined with market testing and judgement about rivals and changing conditions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: give clear predictions of sales at different prices; allow calculation of revenue-maximising prices. Arguments against: estimates may be inaccurate or outdated; rivals' reactions are not included; non-price factors change. Supported judgement: Demand functions are a useful guide but should be combined with market testing and judgement about rivals and changing conditions. items.stem: How is a market demand curve derived from individual demand curves?
options: By averaging individual demand curves
By adding the prices each consumer is willing to pay
By adding the quantities demanded by each consumer at each price (horizontal summation)
By multiplying price by quantity
items.answer: By adding the quantities demanded by each consumer at each price (horizontal summation)
items.markingKey: C. Market demand is the horizontal sum of individual demands.

items.stem: Which of the following would shift the demand curve for electric cars to the right?
options: A rise in the price of electricity
A rise in interest rates on car loans
A fall in the price of electric cars
A rise in the price of petrol
items.answer: A rise in the price of petrol
items.markingKey: D. Petrol cars are substitutes; higher petrol prices make electric cars relatively more attractive.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "law of diminishing marginal utility"?
options: The amount of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at one particular price
The change in quantity demanded resulting from the good becoming relatively cheaper or dearer compared with substitutes
The total satisfaction a consumer gains from consuming a given quantity of a good
As a consumer consumes more units of a good, the extra satisfaction from each additional unit eventually falls
items.answer: As a consumer consumes more units of a good, the extra satisfaction from each additional unit eventually falls
items.markingKey: D. "law of diminishing marginal utility" is as a consumer consumes more units of a good, the extra satisfaction from each additional unit eventually falls.

items.stem: Diego writes: "If 'b' increases, the demand curve shifts to the right." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A change in b changes the slope (responsiveness), not the position; the curve pivots around the quantity intercept.
items.markingKey: A change in b changes the slope (responsiveness), not the position; the curve pivots around the quantity intercept. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between demand and quantity demanded.
items.answer: Demand is the whole relationship between price and quantity (the entire curve); quantity demanded is the amount demanded at one specific price (a point on the curve).
items.markingKey: Demand is the whole relationship between price and quantity (the entire curve); quantity demanded is the amount demanded at one specific price (a point on the curve). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a normal good and an inferior good.
items.answer: Demand for a normal good rises with income; demand for an inferior good falls as income rises because consumers switch to preferred alternatives.
items.markingKey: Demand for a normal good rises with income; demand for an inferior good falls as income rises because consumers switch to preferred alternatives. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the income effect of a fall in the price of rice for a low-income household.
items.answer: A lower price increases the household's real income (purchasing power); for a normal good it can afford to buy more rice and other goods, so quantity demanded rises.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A lower price increases the household's real income (purchasing power); for a normal good it can afford to buy more rice and other goods, so quantity demanded rises. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the price intercept and the quantity intercept.
items.answer: The quantity intercept (a) is quantity demanded when P = 0; the price intercept (a/b) is the price at which quantity demanded falls to zero.
items.markingKey: The quantity intercept (a) is quantity demanded when P = 0; the price intercept (a/b) is the price at which quantity demanded falls to zero. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using the rapid growth of oat milk sales in Europe and the US as an example, explain a change in tastes and preferences as a non-price determinant of demand.
items.answer: Sales of plant-based milks rose strongly in the late 2010s as consumers became more concerned about health, animal welfare and climate change. Changing preferences increased demand for oat milk at every price (rightward shift), while demand for dairy milk fell.
items.markingKey: Context (Sales of plant-based milks rose strongly in the late 2010s as consumers became more concerned about health, animal welfare and climate change.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Changing preferences increased demand for oat milk at every price (rightward shift), while demand for dairy milk fell. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a change in tastes and preferences as a non-price determinant of demand.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate how the law of diminishing marginal utility leads to a downward-sloping demand curve, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram 1: marginal utility (vertical) against quantity consumed (horizontal), a downward-sloping MU curve. Diagram 2: price against quantity, downward-sloping demand. Because each unit gives less extra satisfaction, the price consumers are willing to pay for each extra unit falls, so the demand curve slopes down; the consumer buys up to the point where marginal benefit equals price.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Diagram 1: marginal utility (vertical) against quantity consumed (horizontal), a downward-sloping MU curve. items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate how a change in the price of a complement affects demand for a good, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: Diagram: market for printer ink; a rise in the price of printers reduces the quantity of printers bought, so demand for ink shifts left from D1 to D2; at the original price there is excess supply; price falls from P1 to P2 and quantity from Q1 to Q2.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Price is the most important factor influencing how much of a good consumers buy."
items.answer: Price matters for quantity demanded, but non-price determinants often cause larger changes in demand.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the law of demand shows strong price effects for most goods; firms' pricing strategies work. Arguments against: income, tastes and the prices of substitutes can shift demand substantially; for necessities and addictive goods price has a weak effect; advertising and habits matter (behavioural economics). Supported judgement: Price matters for quantity demanded, but non-price determinants often cause larger changes in demand.

items.stem: "Advertising is the most effective way for firms to increase the demand for their products." Discuss.
items.answer: Advertising can shift demand, especially for differentiated consumer goods, but its effectiveness is limited compared with income and quality changes.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shifts demand right by changing tastes and awareness; builds brand loyalty, making demand less price elastic. Arguments against: income and the prices of substitutes have larger effects; advertising is costly and its effects can be short-lived; product quality, innovation and word of mouth matter more for many goods. Supported judgement: Advertising can shift demand, especially for differentiated consumer goods, but its effectiveness is limited compared with income and quality changes. items.stem: "Marginal utility theory gives a realistic explanation of how consumers make choices." Discuss.
items.answer: The theory is useful for explaining the shape of demand but unrealistic as a description of how people actually decide; behavioural economics adds realism.

items.stem: Using real-world examples, evaluate the view that linear demand functions are too simple to be useful for real-world decision-making.
items.answer: Linear functions are approximations, useful over limited price ranges and for illustrating change, but should be used with caution for large price changes.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: real demand curves are rarely straight lines; many determinants change at once; estimates are uncertain. Arguments against: over a small price range a linear approximation is accurate; simple functions give clear predictions for policy; parameters can be updated with new data.
